bib.title: Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning, Chapter 11: Sampling Methods

question: How can expectations under an intractable probability distribution be approximated by numerical sampling (Monte Carlo) when exact inference is impossible?
contributions: Basic samplers: transformation, rejection, adaptive rejection, importance sampling, SIR (11.1)
Markov chain Monte Carlo: Metropolis, Metropolis-Hastings, Gibbs, slice sampling, hybrid (Hamiltonian) Monte Carlo (11.2-11.5)
Estimating the partition function for model comparison (11.6)

results.claim: In D dimensions, rejection sampling from a Gaussian proposal with a 1% larger standard deviation accepts only about 1 in 20,000 draws at D = 1000, so acceptance falls exponentially with dimension.
results.setup: Zero-mean Gaussian target covariance sigma_p^2 I, zero-mean Gaussian proposal covariance sigma_q^2 I, optimum k = (sigma_q/sigma_p)^D, sigma_q 1% above sigma_p, D = 1000
results.note: (1.01)^1000 is about 20,959, so 1/20,000 is a rounded figure (arithmetic mine, not in the chapter).

results.claim: For the Gaussian worked example the optimum comparison constant is k = (sigma_q/sigma_p)^D, and the acceptance rate is 1/k.
results.setup: Same Gaussian-in-Gaussian rejection sampler, D dimensions, sigma_q >= sigma_p
results.quote: is given by k = (σq/σp)D, as illustrated for D = 1 in Figure 11.7.

results.claim: A random walk Metropolis chain needs order (sigma_max/sigma_min)^2 steps to reach a roughly independent state, because the proposal scale must stay near sigma_min.
results.setup: Isotropic Gaussian proposal, correlated multivariate Gaussian target
results.note: Sec 11.2.2 (p. 542) says the exponent applies to (sigma_max/sigma_min) but also that for a multivariate Gaussian it scales like (sigma_max/sigma_2)^2 with sigma_2 the second-smallest sd (Neal, 1993); the printed 'σ2' is ambiguous with a square.

results.claim: Hybrid Monte Carlo needs leapfrog integration of order sigma_max/sigma_min iterations to reach a nearly independent state, against the square of that ratio for random walk Metropolis.
results.setup: Gaussian target with independent components, step size epsilon below sigma_min
results.quote: number of iterations of order σmax/σmin.

results.claim: Gibbs sampling on a correlated Gaussian needs order (L/l)^2 steps for an independent sample, where l is the conditional width and L the marginal width.
results.setup: Two-variable correlated Gaussian, single-site Gibbs updates

results.claim: A simple random walk over the integers (stay 0.5, step up 0.25, step down 0.25) has E[z^2] = tau/2, so distance grows as sqrt(tau).
In the Metropolis demo (Fig 11.9), 43 of 150 candidate samples were rejected.
results.setup: 2-D Gaussian target, isotropic Gaussian proposal with standard deviation 0.2, single run
results.note: Caption only; seed and start point not given.

results.claim: Ten or twenty independent samples may suffice for an expectation, since estimator variance is var[f]/L and does not depend on the dimension of z.
results.setup: Independent draws from p(z); caveat that MCMC samples are correlated so the effective sample size is smaller
results.quote: In practice, ten or twenty independent samples may

results.claim: Best Cauchy-type proposal for rejection sampling a gamma density uses c = a-1 and b^2 = 2a-1, with k as small as possible.
results.setup: Gamma(z|a,b) with a > 1, proposal q(z) = k/(1+(z-c)^2/b^2) (Eq 11.16), generated as z = b tan y + c
results.note: The gamma rate is also called b (Eq 11.15), reused as the Cauchy width b in Eq 11.16: a symbol clash within the chapter.

results.claim: Gibbs sampling is Metropolis-Hastings with proposal q_k(z*|z) = p(z*_k | z_\k), and its acceptance probability is always 1.
results.setup: Single-component update with other components fixed (Eq 11.49)

results.claim: Importance sampling can give arbitrarily wrong estimates with no diagnostic signal when no sample lands where p(z)f(z) is large.
results.setup: Importance weights r_l = p~(z)/q~(z); apparent variance of weights can look small

limits: Rejection sampling is unsuited to high dimensions: acceptance falls exponentially with D (p. 531-532).
Importance sampling and SIR depend on q(z) matching p(z); weights can be dominated by a few samples, and error may go undetected (p. 534).
Metropolis and Gibbs show random-walk behaviour with poor scaling when length scales differ across directions (pp. 542, 544).
Hybrid Monte Carlo needs a differentiable log density over continuous variables (p. 548) and a leapfrog step size below the smallest length scale (p. 554).
Partition-function ratio estimates need closely matched distributions; chaining is the proposed remedy (pp. 555).
No empirical benchmarks beyond small 1-D and 2-D illustrations; convergence diagnostics are deferred to Robert and Casella (1999), practical advice to Bishop and Nabney (2008) (p. 526).
Dated: 2006. Contains no NUTS, no adaptive step-size or mass-matrix tuning, no variational/SMC comparison beyond Chapter 10 pointers.
practices: Use ancestral sampling for directed graphs with no observed nodes; logic sampling for observed nodes is rarely used because acceptance collapses as observations grow (p. 525).
Choose rejection constant k as small as possible subject to kq(z) >= p~(z) (p. 529).
Use rejection sampling only in one or two dimensions or as a subroutine inside larger algorithms (p. 532).
Normalise importance weights w_l = r_l / sum_m r_m when p and q are known only up to constants (Eq 11.23, p. 533).
Require q(z) not be small or zero where p(z) is significant (p. 534).
Prefer likelihood weighted sampling to uniform sampling for graphical models with evidence (p. 534).
Use SIR instead of rejection sampling when no workable bound k exists (p. 535).
Set Metropolis proposal scale rho of the same order as the smallest length scale sigma_min (p. 542).
Thin the chain by keeping every Mth sample to obtain nearly independent draws (pp. 538, 544).
Verify ergodicity for Gibbs sampling; non-zero conditionals are sufficient (p. 544).
Use over-relaxation, blocking Gibbs or slice sampling to reduce random-walk behaviour or step-size sensitivity (pp. 544-548).
In hybrid Monte Carlo, choose forward or backward integration at random and randomise the step size within a small interval to keep detailed balance and ergodicity (pp. 552-553).
Use chaining with intermediate distributions, ideally one Markov chain run, to estimate partition-function ratios (p. 555).

terms.definition: The quantities r_l = p(z(l))/q(z(l)) correct the bias introduced by sampling from the wrong distribution.
A simpler distribution q(z) from which samples can readily be drawn.
The function kq(z), chosen so that kq(z) >= p~(z) everywhere.
p*(z)T(z,z') = p*(z')T(z',z); a sufficient, not necessary, condition for p* to be invariant.
The distribution of z(m) converges to the invariant distribution regardless of the initial distribution; the invariant distribution is then the equilibrium distribution.
A distribution each step of the chain leaves unchanged.
EM whose E step integral is approximated by a finite sum over samples drawn from p(Z|X, theta_old).
Monte Carlo EM for a finite mixture drawing just one sample per E step, giving a hard assignment.
Alternates an imputation step sampling Z and a posterior step updating the estimate of p(theta|X).
The normalisation constant Z_E of p_E(z) = exp(-E(z))/Z_E, which represents the model evidence.
Half-step momentum update, full-step position update, half-step momentum update; time-reversible and volume-preserving.
Introducing intermediate distributions interpolating a simple distribution with Z known and the target, so Z_M/Z_1 is a product of ratios.
